title: Learning by Confusion Locates a Parametrization-Dependent Fisher Information Maximum
abstract: Learning by confusion (LBC) is a machine-learning method for locating phase transitions without assuming a known order parameter. Its characteristic accuracy curve contains a central maximum that is interpreted as the transition point, but what determines the location and finite-size scaling of this maximum has remained unclear. We derive an exact balance condition for the Bayes-optimal confusion peak and show that, for equilibrium systems with a single swept parameter, the peak closely follows the maximum of the corresponding Fisher information. This immediately gives its finite-size scaling and reveals an unexpected dependence on how the data are sampled: the same configurations arranged on grids uniform in $T$, $\ln T$, or $β=1/T$ can yield different finite-size pseudocritical trajectories. Tests on the Ising, Blume-Capel, Potts, and Baxter-Wu models confirm the prediction across continuous, tricritical, and first-order transitions. Our results identify the statistical quantity measured by LBC and show that finite-size machine-learning estimates can depend on the parametrization of the training data as well as on the underlying physics.
summary: This theoretical paper establishes a deep connection between the 'Learning by Confusion' method for finding phase transitions and the Fisher information. It proves that the LBC peak tracks the Fisher maximum, but critically shows that this estimate can be misleading if the data sampling parametrization is not accounted for.
main_problem: The paper addresses the ambiguity in locating phase transitions using the 'Learning by Confusion' (LBC) method, specifically determining how the peak location relates to established physical quantities.
main_result: The confusion peak location closely follows the maximum of the corresponding Fisher information, and this relationship is shown to be sensitive to how the data are parametrized (e.g., T vs. ln T vs. 1/T).
method: The authors derive an exact balance condition for the Bayes-optimal confusion peak and compare it mathematically to the maximum of the Fisher information, utilizing finite-size scaling analysis.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to classical lattice models exhibiting phase transitions, including the Ising, Blume-Capel, Potts, and Baxter-Wu models, covering continuous, tricritical, and first-order transitions.
key_observables: LBC accuracy ($P(x')$), Bayes error ($E(x')$), Fisher information ($F_x$), and the overlap factor ($c(x)$).
important_parameters: System size ($L$), temperature ($T$), inverse temperature ($ eta$), and the specific parametrization of the data sweep.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the probability distribution belongs to the exponential-family form, and the coincidence of peaks is exact under specific symmetry conditions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of LBC accuracy and Bayes error against the Fisher information for various models and sweeps, confirming the scaling relationship between the two pseudocritical points.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces LBC and the problem of peak location. It then derives the theoretical balance condition linking the confusion peak to the Fisher maximum. The core of the work involves testing this relationship across multiple lattice models and analyzing the dependence on data parametrization.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous mathematical framework connecting machine learning diagnostics (LBC) to fundamental physical quantities (Fisher information) provides a generalizable methodology for analyzing complex, non-equilibrium physical measurements.
